newsitem.title: USA: Cyrix warns over Q2 profits, cites price pressures.
newsitem.headline: Cyrix warns over Q2 profits, cites price pressures.

text.p: Computer chip maker Cyrix Corp. Monday said it expects to post a loss in the second quarter due to weak demand and pricing pressures for its older-generation microprocessors.

Analysts said the news was a further sign of turmoil in the personal computer industry as chipmakers upgrade their products to handle more graphics-intensive applications. The microprocessor is the heart of the PC.

Michael Murphy, editor of the California Technology Stock Letter, said the year is still expected to produce 25 percent year-on-year growth in the PC industry and that individual shortfalls reflected individual difficulties in moving to new products, rather than a broader downturn.
"I don't see this as a big negative (for the industry)," he said. "We're at the inflection point. About mid-August everything starts to pick back up."

Cyrix, which recently introduced a new processor to compete with chip superpower Intel Corp.'s Pentium II, said demand for the new processors has been strong, but pricing pressures on its other chips are expected to drag revenues for the three months ended in June "significantly below" the $75.6 million reported in the first quarter this year.
In the second quarter of 1996, Cyrix posted a second-quarter loss of $16.4 million, or 81 cents per share, on revenues of $27.1 million.
According to First Call, analysts had expected Cyrix to report a profit in the just-completed second quarter of about 7 cents a share.
Cyrix also said it now expects to be around the break-even point for the first half of 1997 vs. a loss of $14.5 million in the same period last year.
"We are disappointed that Cyrix will not reach our goal of profitability in the second quarter," said Jay Swent, chief financial officer and acting chief executive officer.
Cyrix said it shipped more than 35,000 MMX-enhanced 6x86MX processors and that market acceptance of its MediaGX processor continued to meet expectations.
"Looking forward, our current product lineup positions us well to drive both revenue and profit performance in the second half of 1997," he said.
Cyrix's statement comes more than a month after Intel, the world's largest semiconductor maker, issued a similar warning.

In late May, Intel said its second-quarter results would be hurt by weaker demand for some of its older products, particularly in Europe. Intel said second-quarter revenues would be as much as 10 percent below the $6.4 billion reported in the first quarter.

Murphy said that unless Intel's shortfall is even greater than the 10 percent it has projected, the industry should manage the transition to the new chips without damaging overall growth projections for the year.

There may also be a silver lining for Intel's rivals, such as Cyrix and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which have a window of opportunity due to the high demand for new multimedia-ready processors in the second half, he said.
"Because Intel's out of capacity, they're sold out through September on the new stuff, it leaves a window for both AMD and Cyrix ... because Intel cannot possibly build enough chips," Murphy said.
Intel recently cut prices on some of its older-generation chips to make way for new products and is expected to announce another round of steep cuts in late July.
